content: The procurement of medicines is typically managed at a higher administrative level. However, if rifampicin is procured at a peripheral level, it must strictly adhere to the existing policies and guidelines. The community must be educated about the advantages of contact tracing and post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP). It is essential to communicate that single-dose rifampicin (SDR) PEP significantly reduces the risk of developing leprosy. Local advocacy and information, education, and communication (IEC) activities should be conducted periodically if contact tracing or PEP is implemented year-round. Alternatively, these activities should be initiated a few weeks before the actual implementation if they are carried out in a campaign format. This approach ensures maximum coverage. Any additional activities should be determined at the local level. The annual leprosy plan for the district or community level should include all necessary activities for implementing contact tracing and/or PEP. These activities include local advocacy, training or orientation of staff and volunteers, procurement and distribution of rifampicin (preferably alongside multidrug therapy drugs), establishing a referral system, planning for contact tracing, and ensuring monitoring and supervision. It is preferable to integrate contact tracing and PEP into a regular leprosy control plan (or even a broader disease control or health plan) for the district, rather than creating a standalone plan. This integration allows for the monitoring of overall progress in implementing contact tracing and/or PEP as part of leprosy control activities. Monitoring and supervision are essential program management tools designed to track the progress of planned activities and assess the performance of the program or project. Monitoring involves the continuous flow of information within the program chain, supported by periodic or ad-hoc progress reports. It relies on indicators based on SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound) objectives. Only indicators that can be collected with relative ease should be used. The information generated through monitoring is utilized at all management levels (national and sub-national) to assess progress, identify problems, and implement corrective measures. Supervision, on the other hand, focuses on ensuring and improving the quality of services. It primarily involves assessing and enhancing the performance of staff. Supportive supervision fosters improvement through collaboration, setting uniform standards, identifying and solving problems, recognizing needs, and providing opportunities for development. Monitoring and supervision related to contact tracing and PEP can be conducted as part of the overall leprosy program assessment or as part of community outreach activities across public health interventions. Monitoring the implementation of planned activities and supervising the performance of health staff and community health volunteers can be achieved by accompanying them and using checklists and observations. Checklists for various activities include: Enrollment of index cases: Ensuring identified index cases match recorded cases in the treatment register, counseling index cases on leprosy basics, and the benefits of contact tracing and PEP. A sample of index cases may be interviewed to assess their knowledge, and counseling sessions can be observed to ensure quality. Contact listing and tracing: Obtaining consent from index cases for disclosing their disease during contact tracing, ensuring the contact list is as complete as possible, and verifying the accuracy of recorded details. Visits to listed contacts should be made by designated healthcare workers or community health volunteers, and these visits can be cross-checked by visiting a sample of listed contacts. Contact screening: Explaining the importance and steps of screening to contacts, obtaining consent for physical examinations, and ensuring proper screening procedures. Referrals, if any, should be followed up, and contacts who self-report after screening should be enlisted. PEP administration: Counseling contacts about the benefits and limitations of SDR PEP, ensuring exclusion criteria are checked if SDR is provided, and verifying inclusion criteria if SDR is not provided. Supervisors should make efforts to convince contacts who refuse PEP to accept it. Drug management: Ensuring the availability of rifampicin in appropriate dosages as per the anticipated needs of the area or campaign, timely procurement, proper storage according to standard guidelines, and adherence to the first expiry-first out principle. Monitoring of records and reports includes ensuring the completeness and proper maintenance of patient treatment cards, contact lists or registers, and stock records. Reports should be accurately compiled, submitted on time to the next level, and feedback, if any, should be acted upon. Indicators for assessing the implementation of contact screening and/or PEP include: The number of index cases enrolled during a specific period. The number of contacts listed against these index cases. The average number of contacts per index case. The number and proportion of contacts screened. The number and proportion of contacts who received SDR. The number of leprosy cases detected among contacts during the period. The proportion of leprosy cases detected as part of contact tracing. The rate of leprosy case detection among listed contacts. These indicators can be collected monthly, quarterly, or annually for a given area and aggregated at a higher level. Supervisors can compare their findings with routine reporting data to assess the quality of reporting. Information, education, and communication (IEC) are critical components of any public health program. An informed community fosters demand for services, and well-informed patients or affected individuals are more likely to comply and cooperate. Simple messages such as Leprosy can now be prevented or A single dose of rifampicin can significantly reduce the risk of developing leprosy should be highlighted in a language understood by the beneficiaries, avoiding medical jargon. These messages provide hope to patients, their families, contacts, and the broader community.
